title: Apple Mac Studio M5 Ultra and Mac Mini M6 Launched
gist: Apple's new Mac Studio M5 Ultra (up to 512GB unified memory, 1.2TB/s bandwidth) and Mac mini M6 push local AI inference capacity further, but pricing has jumped meaningfully and NVIDIA's ~$100K GB300 Station still offers several times more memory bandwidth for those who need serious throughput.

insights.claim: The Apple M6 chip in the new Mac mini is Apple's first 2nm desktop part, targeting the mainstream desktop segment with a 12-core CPU (2 super cores, 4 performance cores, 6 efficiency cores), a 12-core GPU with a Neural Accelerator in each core, and a dual 16-core Neural Engine.
insights.speaker: Vic A
insights.so_what: First 2nm process node in a desktop Apple Silicon part signals TSMC's 2nm ramp is now feeding consumer desktop silicon, relevant for tracking TSMC leading-edge node adoption timelines.
insights.locator: The Apple M6 brings a 12-core CPU split into two super cores, four performance cores, and six efficiency cores.

insights.claim: The M6 Mac mini tops out at 32GB of unified memory with up to 170GB/s of bandwidth, and Apple claims 1.2x faster multithreaded CPU performance than M5, nearly 30 percent more peak GPU AI compute, 10 percent more memory bandwidth, and up to 2x peak compute on its dual Neural Engine versus prior generations.
insights.speaker: Vic A
insights.so_what: 32GB memory ceiling keeps the M6 mini positioned for mainstream/consumer use rather than local large-model AI workloads, which require the higher-memory Ultra tier.
insights.quote: Apple claims 1.2x faster multithreaded CPU performance than M5, nearly 30 percent more peak GPU AI compute, and 10 percent more memory bandwidth.
insights.locator: Unified memory tops out at 32GB with up to 170GB/s of bandwidth.

insights.claim: The Apple M5 Ultra uses Apple's UltraFusion technology to join two dual-die M5 Max chips into one quad-die SoC via an inter-die fabric rated above 4.4TB/s, scaling to a 36-core CPU (12 super cores, 24 performance cores), an 80-core GPU with Neural Accelerators, and a 32-core Neural Engine.
insights.speaker: Vic A
insights.so_what: Confirms Apple's continued reliance on chiplet-fusion (UltraFusion) rather than a monolithic die to scale its top-end desktop silicon, a design pattern worth tracking against competitors' chiplet strategies.
insights.locator: Apple UltraFusion ties two dual-die M5 Max chips into one quad-die SoC.

insights.claim: The M5 Ultra supports up to 512GB of unified memory served by 1.2TB/s of bandwidth — 50 percent higher than the M3 Ultra — and Apple claims up to 1.3x faster multithreaded performance versus the M3 Ultra (based on preproduction parts); it also adds a PCIe Gen6 SSD, faster than SSDs currently available on the market.
insights.speaker: Vic A
insights.so_what: 512GB at 1.2TB/s bandwidth is the key spec enabling on-device inference of very large language models that don't fit on typical discrete GPU memory — a differentiator investors in the local-AI-hardware space should track against next-gen unified-memory competitors.
insights.quote: Unified memory still supports up to 512GB but is served by 1.2TB/s of bandwidth, which Apple says is 50 percent higher than the M3 Ultra.
insights.locator: The M5 Ultra is the larger of the pair.

insights.claim: The author frames the Mac Studio M5 Ultra as continuing the prior M3 Ultra's role as 'the big local AI play' — its large unified memory pool holds large language models that common discrete GPUs cannot fit, and the higher 1.2TB/s bandwidth should improve tokens-per-second for on-device inference.
insights.speaker: Vic A
insights.so_what: Reinforces Mac Studio's niche as the go-to prosumer/small-business platform for running large local models without cloud GPU costs, a competitive consideration for anyone selling local-inference hardware or software tooling.
insights.quote: We called the prior M3 Ultra Mac Studio the big local AI play.
insights.locator: We called the prior M3 Ultra Mac Studio the big local AI play.

insights.claim: Apple's pricing for its top-memory desktop has risen meaningfully: the author paid around $10K for a Mac Studio M3 Ultra with 512GB, while the new 256GB M5 Ultra model costs over $11K — and the 512GB M5 Ultra variant won't ship until October, so its price isn't yet known.
insights.speaker: Vic A
insights.so_what: A roughly 10%+ price increase for half the memory capacity signals Apple is pushing pricing power on its highest-margin desktop tier — worth watching for how the eventual 512GB M5 Ultra price lands and what it implies for Apple's Mac segment ASPs/margins.
insights.quote: An Apple Mac Studio M3 Ultra 512GB we purchased for around $10K, but the 256GB M5 Ultra model is over $11K.

insights.claim: The author contrasts the Mac Studio M5 Ultra with NVIDIA's GB300 Station desk-side AI system, priced around $100K, which offers an NVIDIA GPU with several times higher memory bandwidth and more total system memory than the Mac Studio.
insights.speaker: Vic A
insights.so_what: Frames Apple's local-AI desktop as a budget-tier alternative to NVIDIA's far pricier desk-side AI systems rather than a direct performance competitor — investors should size Apple's local-AI opportunity as complementary/lower-tier to NVIDIA's high-end desk-side compute, not substitutive.
insights.quote: the NVIDIA GB300 Station line is about $100K but offers an NVIDIA GPU with several times higher memory bandwidth and more total system memory
insights.locator: Something worth considering is that, from a desk-side AI perspective.

insights.claim: The author benchmarked an NVIDIA GB300 Station running a Qwen3.6-35B-A3B NVFP4 Fast model at over 26,000 tokens/s at a concurrency of 512, illustrating the throughput gap versus Apple's unified-memory desktop platforms.
insights.speaker: Vic A
insights.so_what: Gives a concrete real-world throughput data point for NVIDIA's desk-side AI hardware, useful as a benchmark reference when comparing local-inference platforms across vendors.
insights.quote: We had a Qwen3.6-35B-A3B NVFP4 Fast model running at well over 26K tokens/s at c=512, which is wild to see.
insights.locator: We had a Qwen3.6-35B-A3B NVFP4 Fast model running at well over 26K tokens/s.
